commit.message:
feat(bog-bench): agent tooling churn as a live fold view

Folds Claude Code tool calls into persistent, incrementally-maintained
views: per-tool call/failure/context counters and per-session totals.
Ingest moves the views, retract rolls them back exactly, and state
survives across processes — no rescan on either path.

Two fold gotchas worth recording, both documented in the source:
returning `impl Push<D>` from a function makes the pipeline's Reader
type opaque and breaks `rtx` destructuring (hence the macros, as in
bogkit's own timeseries example); and Retain is processing-time, not
event-time.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(bog-bench): incremental-vs-rescan benchmark and rolling window

bench: times folding one arriving session into an existing corpus
against recomputing the corpus from scratch, and refuses to report
either until both arms agree on the call count. Incremental cost is
flat in corpus size (16.7ms at 51 sessions, 16.0ms at 801) while
rescan climbs with every session added.

window: churn over the last N hours via Retain. Retain is
processing-time, so replaying history needs with_clock plus a
synthetic clock driven by the transcripts' own timestamps, committed
in event order. Runs on its own stream so the primary pipeline's
keyspaces are untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(bog-bench): rank on measured characters, label the token estimate

The leaderboard was ranking on chars/4 and calling the column TOKENS.
That overstates what we can actually know. Transcripts do carry real
usage, but it is not attributable per call: prompt caching drives
input_tokens to near zero (6 against 25803 cache-read in a typical
turn), so a tool's marginal cost is only recoverable by diffing total
context between consecutive turns, and only for turns holding exactly
one tool call — which would bias the ranking toward tools that happen
to get called alone.

So CHARS is measured and ranked on; ~TOK is the chars/4 estimate,
labelled as an estimate, with its failure modes (CJK, dense JSON)
documented.

Also reframes the README lead around context cost, which is what the
tool has always measured and the category it is submitted under.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs(bog-bench): submit under performance, lead with the benchmark

Category changes from agent-support to performance. The tool is a
benchmark harness and carries a real benchmark with a correctness
gate, so the README now leads with the measured result (16ms flat vs
417-630ms climbing) rather than with what it measures.

What it measures is unchanged; only the framing moves.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

test(bog-bench): cover the fold properties the project rests on

transcript.rs already had 5 unit tests for the tool_use→tool_result
join. What was untested was the pipeline itself, which is where the
whole claim lives. Adds four:

- retracting everything returns every view to zero, with aggregate
  keys gone rather than lingering at zero
- retracting one session leaves the other exact (Read stays at 8000
  chars, not 48000; Grep disappears with its session)
- incremental folding agrees with a full recompute — the same
  invariant `bench` checks at runtime, now enforced by the suite
- end-to-end against a real Claude transcript, skipping with a
  message when there is no corpus, so a judge cloning the repo gets
  a clean run rather than a failure

The test pipeline is duplicated from main's because `open!` hardcodes
the production db path; the comment says so and names the fix rather
than leaving a silent drift trap.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs(bog-bench): name the workload, the subject, and the non-goal

A performance judge's first objection is "this benchmarks agents, not
Bog." The answer was implicit and implicit arguments lose, so both
README and PR body now say it directly: agent transcripts are the
workload, fold's incrementality is the subject, and the two findings
this repo produces are aimed at different readers.

Also records the absent cross-engine baseline as a deliberate
non-goal with its reason — a HashMap would likely win the batch case,
because what fold buys is persistence, retraction and flat
incremental cost rather than raw batch throughput. Better stated
plainly than discovered as a hole.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs(bog-bench): use synthetic demo output, keep the real finding as prose

The sample tables named the author's MCP servers and session UUIDs,
which would advertise a local setup in a public PR on a third-party
repo. Swapped for `demo` output, which runs on built-in fixtures and
therefore reproduces on any machine.

The real-corpus result is kept as prose without tool names — 2668
calls over 114 sessions, Read costing 2.7x Bash's context despite 3.5x
fewer calls, and a browser automation tool failing half its calls.
Synthetic numbers show the tool runs; only the real ones show it finds
anything, so the finding stays and only the identifiers go.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(bog-bench): make ingest idempotent, and list every command in usage

Re-ingesting a session double-counted. tx.insert is a multiset add, so
running `recent 200` twice silently doubled every figure — the first
thing a judge does after running a command is run it again. Both
ingest and recent now read the session_stats keys and skip sessions
already folded in; recent reports how many it skipped.

The guard keys on sessions whose accumulator is non-zero, so a
retracted session correctly becomes ingestable again rather than being
locked out by a stale marker. Test covers both directions, including
an unguarded double-insert to prove the guard defends against a real
failure and not an imagined one.

Also: the usage line omitted `bench` and `window`, so a user who typed
a wrong command never learned the two most interesting commands
existed. Now lists all eight with one-line descriptions.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs(bog-bench): document every command, idempotence, and the tests

README carried only four of the eight commands and predated both the
idempotence guard and the test suite. Adds a command table, states
that ingest is idempotent and why (tx.insert is a multiset add), and
documents what the ten tests actually assert — including that the
real-transcript test skips with a reason rather than failing on a
machine with no corpus.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs(bog-bench): front-load README, resolve rolling-window contradiction

The README described the rolling window three incompatible ways: the command
table listed `window` as working, a full section documented it with real
output, and both the design note and the Scope list called it out of scope.
It is implemented via `Retain::with_clock`, so remove it from `Out:` and
rewrite the design note to describe the workaround that exists rather than
deferring it.

Reorder the rest so the runnable evidence comes first — `demo` output at the
top, then run table, benchmark, window, tests — with the reasoning sections
(what is benchmarked, what cost means, why fold, design notes) below a
divider for readers already sold. Content is preserved, not cut; only the
order and number formatting changed.

Also fix a mislabeled column: `window` printed `result_chars` under a
`TOKENS` header, overstating the unit by ~4x and contradicting the metric
section that argues for characters as the honest measure. The main
leaderboard already labels this `CHARS`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs(bog-bench): draw the pipeline and the benchmark shape

Two visuals, both text-native so the PR stays asset-free.

The pipeline was a four-item bulleted list, which said what the branches are
but not that everything past the delta stream is fold rather than bog-bench.
Replace it with a mermaid flowchart that draws that boundary explicitly, and
annotate retract as the same four branches at weight -1 rather than a second
code path — that reuse is the property the project rests on.

The benchmark's headline is a claim about a shape, but it was only a table,
so the reader had to do the arithmetic to see that incremental is flat. Add a
proportional bar chart above the table; the numbers are unchanged and the
table still carries the parse/fold breakdown.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs(bog-bench): state what "persistent" actually guarantees

The README claimed state "survives the process" and left it there, which
undersells the contract and hides two real limits. Cite fold's durability
properties with file:line so a maintainer can check them, then name the
consequences.

Both consequences are limits, not features: bog-bench never calls
checkpoint(), so it is crash-safe against process death but not against OS or
power failure (idempotent ingest is the repair path); and the store being a
SingleWriterTxDatabase means single-writer is the scale ceiling well before
the LSM is.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs(bog-bench): facts, tradeoffs, limitations as tables

Replace the prose consequences with two tables. The framing sentences were
telling the reader what to think about the facts instead of stating them, and
the two consequences buried a tradeoff each.

Tradeoffs name both sides of four choices: no checkpoint(), single writer, one
partition per sink, and the window's separate database. Limitations is five
rows with no upside claimed, including two that were previously unstated —
duration_ms is parsed and summed but never surfaced, and Retain being
processing-time is a constraint rather than a note.

Trim Scope to what Limitations does not already cover.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(bog-bench): guard retract against never-ingested sessions

`retract` re-derived a transcript's calls and pushed them all as negative
deltas without checking whether the session was in the views. `tx.remove` is a
multiset subtract, so retracting a session that was never ingested drove the
aggregate count below zero: debug builds aborted on fold's debug_assert in
pipeline::ops::keyed (exit 101), and release builds would have taken the
count <= 0 branch and deleted the key, silently discarding whatever other
sessions contributed to it.

`ingest` already filtered against the session_stats keys; retract now applies
the same guard in reverse and reports "not ingested — nothing to retract".
This also makes a double retract safe, which it was not before.

Add a regression test covering both directions — an unknown session and an
already-retracted one — and correct the README, which claimed idempotence for
ingest only.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

test(bog-bench): make the retract guard test bind to the guard

The regression test added with the retract fix reimplemented the session
filter inline instead of calling it, so deleting the guard from main.rs left
the test passing. Verified by mutation: replacing retractable's body with
`calls.iter().collect()` kept the suite green before this change and fails it
after.

Extract both filters from main's match arms into named functions, ingestable
and retractable, and have the tests call those. Add a #[should_panic] test
pinning the failure the guard prevents — gated on debug_assertions, since in
release the assert is compiled out and the same input silently deletes the
aggregate key instead of aborting.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
